source: Weller et al. (2024) When do generative query and document expansions fail? A comprehensive study across methods, retrievers, and datasets
finding: Across 11 LLM expansion methods (query-side such as HyDE, document-side such as Doc2Query, and combined), 12 datasets and 24 retrieval models, expansion helps weak retrievers and hurts strong ones. Gain falls as the baseline score rises. Error analysis: the damage comes from added terms that dilute the relevance signal.
numbers: Strong negative correlation between baseline nDCG@10 and gain from expansion (Figure 1). Hand check of 30 failures: 2 were unjudged relevant documents, the other 28 were all due to irrelevant or wrong keywords added by the expansion. Exception: on ArguAna (long queries) expansion helps because it shortens the query.
quote: expansion improves scores for weaker models, but generally harms stronger models
limits: Ad hoc document retrieval benchmarks (TREC DL, FiQA, ArguAna and others), not agent memory. No random-token control. Model strength is confounded with model size.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 6. Enrichment at write time or query time is not free: with a strong retriever or reader it can add noise. Test any enrichment against a plain-note arm and against same-length filler.

source: Cuconasu et al. (2024) The Power of Noise: Redefining Retrieval for RAG Systems (SIGIR 2024)
finding: Passages that are semantically close to the question but lack the answer (distracting) hurt the LLM a lot. Random unrelated passages added to the prompt, placed next to the question, did not hurt and sometimes raised accuracy. So a mismatched but semantically strong item costs more than an unrelated item.
numbers: Llama2-7b on NQ-open: gold-only accuracy 0.5642; with 1, 2, 4 distractors chosen by the ADORE hard-negative retriever: 0.4068, 0.3815, 0.3626 (all lower; significant by Wilcoxon p<.01 in the main table). Closed-book Llama2 0.1123. Adding random documents next to the query raised accuracy by 0.08 (+36%) in the best oracle setting; with 4 retrieved documents plus random fill, up to +0.07 (+35%). Random word-salad documents also helped relative to random Wikipedia. Falcon did not gain in the oracle setting.
limits: Models are 2023-era (Llama2-7b, MPT, Phi-2, Falcon) with 2048-4096 token limits. Random documents sit in the prompt, not in the stored note, so this does not test write-time padding directly. Mechanism of the random-document gain is unclear.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 3. Extra tokens alone are not harmless or helpful by default; semantic closeness without the answer is the harmful kind. A write-time enrichment test needs both a random-token arm and a near-miss-key arm.

source: Amiraz et al. (2025) The Distracting Effect: Understanding Irrelevant Passages in RAG
finding: Defines the distracting effect of a passage as the probability the LLM answers instead of abstaining when shown only that irrelevant passage. The score is stable across LLMs. Hard distracting passages cost 6 to 11 accuracy points when added next to a gold passage, more than weak distractors, and the cost persists for a 70B model. Fine-tuning on hard distractors helped.
numbers: Hard-distractor threshold DE>0.8, weak DE<0.2. Accuracy drop from hard distractors 6 to 11 points depending on LLM (Llama-3.3-70B included). Fine-tuning on hard distractors: up to +7.5% answer accuracy over fine-tuning on conventional RAG data.
limits: Open models up to 70B, short-answer QA. Fine-tuning result is training, not scaffolding.
agent_relevance: Gap 3. Closest LLM analogue of Thomson and Tulving's strong-but-wrong cue: the cost is real (6-11 points) but smaller than the human drop, and it is measurable per passage, so an agent could score its own retrieved notes for distraction.

source: Cuconasu et al. (2025) Do RAG Systems Really Suffer From Positional Bias?
finding: The lost-in-the-middle effect interacts with match quality. In a controlled test, hard distractors do more harm at the start or end of the prompt than in the middle, so the position effect applies to distractors too. In real retrieval, relevant and highly distracting passages are both near the top, the two effects cancel, and rearranging passages by LLM position preference does no better than random shuffling.
numbers: Over 60% of queries have at least one highly distracting passage in the top 10 retrieved. Distracting effect of a hard distractor: 36-44% at edge slots versus 28-34% in middle slots (Qwen 2.5 7B). Hard distractor costs about 6 accuracy points on average versus weak distractors only, more at the worst slot. Controlled position effect up to 5 points. Top-5 accuracy, Qwen 7B with BGE+rerank: sequential 68.53, inverse 71.33, shuffle 71.00, max-relevance order 71.73, min-distraction order 70.80; Llama 70B 74.33 to 75.47.
limits: Short-answer QA on three benchmarks, models 3B to 70B. Passages are retrieved documents, not agent lessons.
agent_relevance: Gap 10. Placing a matched lesson in a model-favoured slot is not a reliable gain, because a mismatched near-neighbour may land in the same slot. Put effort into filtering mismatched items, not into ordering.

source: Yuan, Su, Yao (2026) Diagnosing Retrieval vs. Utilization Bottlenecks in LLM Agent Memory (ICLR 2026)
finding: A 3x3 study on LoCoMo crosses write strategy (raw 3-turn chunks, Mem0-style fact extraction, MemGPT-style session summaries) with retrieval method (cosine, BM25, hybrid rerank). Retrieval method dominates. Storing the raw text, in the form the question will be asked in, matches or beats the LLM-rewritten forms. Extracted facts with BM25 was worst, which fits a form mismatch between query words and stored words.
numbers: GPT-5-mini, text-embedding-3-small, k=5, 1,540 non-adversarial questions. Accuracy cosine/BM25/hybrid: raw chunks 77.9/59.2/81.1; extracted facts 72.2/49.4/77.3; summaries 70.1/62.7/73.3. Averages by retrieval 73.4/57.1/77.2. Retrieval precision@5 vs accuracy r=0.98. Failure modes: retrieval failure 11-46% of questions (46.3% for BM25 with extracted facts), utilization failure 4-8%, hallucination 0.4-1.4%. Hybrid halves retrieval failure (35.3% to 11.4% for raw chunks).
limits: One backbone, one benchmark, one run per cell, k=5 only. Write strategies are lossy rewrites, not additive enrichment, so it does not test adding keys to a raw note. The form-mismatch reading of the BM25 result is ours, not the authors'.
agent_relevance: Gap 2 and 6. For dialogue memory the rewrite-at-write step does not pay; keeping the original wording plus a better retriever does. Favours write-time additions kept alongside the raw text over replacing it.

source: Smith and Handy (2014) Effects of varied and constant environmental contexts on acquisition and retention (JEP:LMC)
finding: Varying the background context across retrieval-practice trials made memories independent of the study context: worse during practice but better at a delayed test with no matching context. Restudy in varied contexts gave no such benefit. So decontextualisation needs retrieval practice, not just repeated exposure.
numbers: Exp 1 (N=45, face-name pairs over video scenes, final test 2 days later with new scenes): final recall constant .43 vs varied .61, t(43)=2.29, d=.71; forgetting from last practice to final test constant .50 vs varied .02, d=2.34. Exp 2 (N=48, no context at test): practice better for constant, F(1,46)=13.79. Exp 3 (N=21, same-day test) also favoured varied at final recall. Exp 4 (N=36, restudy instead of retrieval practice): final recall constant .51 vs varied .36, ns (t(34)=1.72, p=.095); Day 2 .45 vs .30 after excluding retested pairs, ns (p=.126).
limits: Video scenes, face-name pairs, university students, 2 days. Authors read it as the new theory of disuse (low retrieval strength at practice builds storage strength), not encoding variability. Small cells (9 to 18 per group in Exp 3 and 4).
agent_relevance: Gap 7 closed for humans. A lesson retrieved and used under many task contexts, with real retrieval attempts, should become cue-independent. Re-reading the note in many contexts will not. Agent version untested.

source: Murre (2021) The Godden and Baddeley (1975) experiment on context-dependent memory on land and underwater: a replication (R. Soc. Open Sci.), design notes on the original
finding: Murre's description of the original: Experiment 1 used 16 undergraduate amateur divers, each in all four land/water learn-test combinations, 4 days of diving. The original interaction was F=22.0 (p<.001, df2=12). Original cell means were not in the text that was read, so the founding means are still unextracted.
numbers: Original: N=16, interaction F=22.0, eta2=.647, d lower bound 2.708. Replication: 16 Amsterdam divers (10 men, 6 women, mean age 29.5), all four conditions in about 1.5 h instead of 4 days, filmed for TV, 180 Dutch words; no interaction (F=1.999, p=.163).
limits: Secondhand for the original. Replication differs in procedure (1.5 h vs 4 days, proactive interference, TV crew). Its preregistration was filed after data analysis (in-principle acceptance only).
agent_relevance: Gap 8, partly. Treat the diver result as a weak anchor. Do not quote diver numbers from secondary pages.

source: Berglund et al. (2024) The Reversal Curse, Appendix B.6 in-context results (ICLR 2024)
finding: The cue-direction failure is parametric. When the fact is placed in the prompt, GPT-3 reverses it almost perfectly with three demonstrations. A footnote says the Reversal Curse does not apply to in-context learning.
numbers: 3-shot GPT-3 in-context accuracy: NameToDescription 100 at 350M, 1.3B, 6.7B, 175B; DescriptionToName 96.67 at 350M and 100 at the larger sizes. Finetuned (Table 6, 350M): same direction 9.8 and 99.9, reverse direction 0.0 for both.
limits: Short context with three demonstrations; the fact is one statement. Not long-context retrieval, not 2024-2026 models. Search snippets mention arXiv 2512.25026 and an ACL 2026 paper on reversed-order queries in controlled graphs; those were not opened.
agent_relevance: Gap 9, partly closed. Text placed in the prompt is not cue-direction locked in the short-context case. Retrieval has to find the note, but once it is in the prompt the reader can use it from either side. Long-context and many-note case still open.

source: Yoran et al. (2024) Making Retrieval-Augmented Language Models Robust to Irrelevant Context (ICLR 2024)
finding: Retrieved context that does not fit the question can lower accuracy below no-retrieval, and the wrong answer often copies an entity from the mismatched passage. A small NLI model that checks whether the question-answer pair is entailed by the context prevents the loss but throws away some useful passages. Training on mixed relevant and irrelevant contexts made the model robust with about 1,000 examples.
numbers: Llama-2-13B few-shot on 5 QA sets: random retrieved context dropped the In-Context RALM by more than 10 points on average; NLI filtering mitigated it. Manual check of 240 failures: retrieval caused the error in 73% (65-85% by setting). With low-ranked context the wrong entity was in the retrieved text in 77% of NQ errors, 37% with random context. Retrieval exemplars hurt: the no-retrieval exemplar prompt beat retrieval exemplars by over 2 points on average even when retrieving at test.
limits: Llama-2-13B and 70B, 2023. Forced-answer-then-score was not tested; the filter uses an external NLI model. Top-1 Google results hurt on StrategyQA and Fermi.
agent_relevance: Gap 5. A post-hoc fit check on the retrieved item before use works, the LLM version of Higham's monitoring step. It costs useful items, as in the human forced-report trade-off. Not tested on frontier models.

source: Yu et al. (2024) Chain-of-Note: Enhancing Robustness in Retrieval-Augmented Language Models (EMNLP 2024)
finding: Writing a short reading note on each retrieved document, judging its relevance to the question before answering, makes the reader more robust to noisy documents and more willing to say unknown. This is a forced relevance judgement before the answer.
numbers: LLaMa-2 7B fine-tuned on 10K GPT-4-written note examples, DPR retrieval on NQ, TriviaQA, WebQ and RealTimeQA. With 100% noisy documents average exact match improved by +7.9; with 0% noise +2.7. Rejection rate on real-time questions beyond training knowledge +10.5. Abstract also reports GPT-4 with CoN beats chain-of-thought.
limits: Main gain is from training a 7B model, not prompting. The GPT-4 prompting claim was only read in the abstract.
agent_relevance: Gap 5. Cheap scaffold version: before using a retrieved lesson, write one line on whether its stated conditions match the present task. The 'cues are associates' warning of Santa and Lamwers has no direct LLM test yet.

source: Wang et al. (2025) Astute RAG: Overcoming Imperfect Retrieval Augmentation and Knowledge Conflicts for LLMs
finding: With Claude 3.5 Sonnet and Gemini 1.5 Pro, imperfect retrieval is common and sometimes worse than no retrieval. When every retrieved passage is wrong, plain RAG is more than 50 points below no-RAG. A prompt-only method that first elicits the model's own knowledge, then consolidates internal and external passages with source labels, is the only one that stays near the no-RAG level.
numbers: About 70% of retrieved passages did not contain the true answer; 19.2% of items showed an internal-external conflict (Claude 3.5 Sonnet); in conflicts internal knowledge was right 47.4% and external 52.6%. Worst-case RGB (all passages negative): RAG vs no-RAG gap above 50 points. Astute RAG about 80% correct on the conflict subset; relative improvement over the best baseline 6.85% (Claude) and 4.13% (Gemini). On NQ and TriviaQA, RAG lagged no-RAG for advanced LLMs.
limits: Short-answer QA, several LLM calls per question (token cost not compared with a single pass). Authors' own method.
agent_relevance: Gap 3 and 5. First frontier-model evidence that mismatched retrieval can cost far more than 3 points: in the all-wrong case, over 50. A source-aware consolidation step before use is a prompt-only fix.

finding: Prepending a short LLM-written explanation of where a chunk sits in its document, at index time, cuts failed retrievals. The added context is part of the stored text, so it is matched at retrieval even though the query does not carry the scene.
numbers: Top-20 chunk failure rate: baseline 5.7%; contextual embeddings 3.7% (35% fewer); contextual embeddings plus contextual BM25 2.9% (49% fewer); plus reranking from top 150 to top 20 1.9% (67% fewer). About $1.02 per million document tokens one-time with prompt caching (800-token chunks, about 100 tokens of context per chunk). Datasets: codebases, fiction, arXiv papers, science papers.
limits: Vendor blog read through a page-fetch tool that summarises, not peer reviewed, averaged across datasets. No random-prefix control and no split of gain between extra words and document-specific context. Not a scene-absent-at-retrieval test.
agent_relevance: Gap 1 and 2, partly. Adds an index-time arm with real numbers: about 100 tokens per item, a large failure cut at top-20. The needed control (same-length random or wrong-document prefix) is still missing.

source: Yoon et al. (2025) Hypothetical Documents or Knowledge Leakage? Rethinking LLM-based Query Expansion
finding: HyDE and Query2doc gains in fact verification are concentrated in claims where the generated text already contains a sentence entailed by the gold evidence. When it does not, performance is below the unexpanded baseline. So rewriting the query toward the stored form helps only when the model's guess of the stored form is right.
numbers: Seven LLMs, three benchmarks (FEVER, SciFact, AVeriTeC). GPT-4o-mini HyDE on FEVER: 83.5% of claims had an entailed sentence in the generated document; Gemini-1.5-flash HyDE on SciFact only 27.6%. FEVER Recall@5 with GPT-4o-mini HyDE: matched claims 40.0, unmatched 23.4, all 37.3, Contriever baseline 26.8. Query2doc FEVER Recall@5: matched 40.5, unmatched 23.8, all 36.4, BM25 baseline 31. Differences significant at p<.001.
limits: Fact verification on Wikipedia-type corpora the LLM has probably seen. Authors call this knowledge leakage; on private stores the benefit may be smaller.
agent_relevance: Gap 6. Query rewriting (HyDE) is a bet on the stored form. For private agent notes the model has not seen the stored text, so storing several forms at write time is likely safer. No head-to-head on agent memory found.

source: Thomson (1984) Citation Classic commentary on Thomson and Tulving (1970), Current Contents
finding: Thomson says he ran the 1970 study to refute Tulving's claim that strong associates do not help unless encoded. The result supported Tulving instead. Lists the founding series with citation counts: Tulving and Osler 1968 (J Exp Psychol 77:593-601, cited 150 times by 1984), Tulving and Thomson 1971 (160), Tulving and Thomson 1973 Psych Rev 80:352-73 (600).
numbers: Thomson and Tulving 1970 J Exp Psychol 86:255-62, cited over 170 times by 1984. No effect sizes in the commentary.
limits: Commentary, no data. Useful for the adversarial origin: the test was designed to disconfirm.
agent_relevance: Gap 8, bibliographic only. Exact N and means of Tulving and Osler 1968 and Tulving and Thomson 1973 were not obtained (paywalled; search budget ran out).

source: Smith (1986) Environmental context-dependent recognition memory using a short-term memory task for input (Memory and Cognition 14:347-354)
finding: Environmental context effects on recognition appeared in three experiments when the input task was a short-term memory task, though almost all earlier studies found no context effect for recognition. Material studied for a long-term memory test was not susceptible to background context; material only maintained for a short-term test was.
numbers: Exp 1 (df 32, so N=36): different-context subjects made about 50% more recognition errors than same-context. Exp 2: different-context errors 28% (1.21 errors) higher, F(1,104)=4.36, p<.05. A free-recall check showed a robust test-context effect, F(1,56).
limits: Only partly extracted (output cut by a disk-full error). Small effects on errors; student samples; rooms as context.
agent_relevance: Gap 7 and boundary condition. How an item is processed at input decides whether context binds to it. Notes written as deliberate long-term records may bind less to the writing scene than quick scratch notes.

source: Search snippets only: Hutter et al. 'Lost but not only in the middle'; arXiv 2512.25026 (in-context reversal probe); ACL 2026 reversed-order graph study; arXiv 2512.14313 (dynamic context selection)
finding: Snippets say: position effects depend on distractor type and context length (Hutter); a controlled-graph study shows large drops on reversed-order queries and blames surface co-occurrence (ACL 2026); a Dec 2025 paper places relevant passages at start, middle and end with distractors. None was read.
limits: Not opened. Do not cite numbers from these.
agent_relevance: Leads for gap 9 and 10 in a later pass.
